title: Ask URA Commissioner General 37 - Uganda Revenue Authority
text:
# Ask URA Commissioner General 37
When is the transition from TIN to NIN commencing?
Dear Reader,
On 1 September 2026, Cabinet approved the use of the National Identification Number (NIN) issued by the National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA) as the primary Tax Identification Number (TIN) for individuals.
Section 4 of the Tax Procedures Code Act introduced, the NIN will serve as the tax identifier for individuals, while the Entity Registration Number (ERN) or Business Registration Number (BRN) will serve as the tax identifiers for non-individuals.
The transition has already commenced with the mapping of taxpayers NINs to their respective TIN. This is being undertaken through the following three main avenues;
URA-initiated engagements: Taxpayers are contacted through email and requested to provide their NINs, which are then manually updated by URA officials.
Walk-in services: Taxpayers provide their NINs when accessing URA service centres.
URA web portal: The NIN update option has been made mandatory for Ugandan taxpayers who have not yet updated their NINs when they attempt to access URA online services.
To support this transition, the Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) encourages all taxpayers whose NIN is not mapped to their TIN to update their records through the available channels as soon as possible.
At full rollout, TINs will no longer be recognised as taxpayer login identifiers. Taxpayers who have not completed the transition by that time will therefore be unable to access the URA system until their details are updated.
Why did we need to shift from TIN to NIN?
Dear Reader,
The primary objective of the transition from the Tax Identification Number (TIN) to the National Identification Number (NIN) is to curb the fragmented approach across multiple government agencies managing different categories of registration under various legal frameworks. The need to align data inconsistencies and repetitive data requirements across agencies has resulted in adopting the National Identification Number (NIN) as the unique identifier for individual taxpayers as a measure to close these gaps.
Other key reasons for the transition include:
Improving service efficiency by eliminating multiple verification processes that often lead to delays and inconvenience for taxpayers.
Strengthening taxpayer compliance monitoring through accurate identification and verification of taxpayer information.
Enhancing data integrity by creating a more reliable and coordinated taxpayer database across government systems.
Consistent Identification which ensures continuity, remaining unchanged even when a taxpayer’s personal details — such as names, addresses or other biographical information are updated. This minimises confusion and results in more accurate identification, particularly in cases involving individuals with similar names, corporate mergers, or the use of trade names.
Improved Communication through provision of a clear, consistent reference point that strengthens communication between URA and taxpayers across both digital and traditional channels, reducing friction and streamlining interactions.
A single identifier used across Government will improve service delivery and communication with taxpayers.
Strengthened national identification system, which improves visibility into economic actors and reduces illicit financial activity and revenue leakage.
What benefits are we meant to derive from the NIN to TIN Change?
Dear Reader,
The transition from the Tax Identification Number (TIN) to the National Identification Number (NIN) is expected to deliver several benefits to taxpayers and the government, including:
Unified Identification: Your national identity and tax identity will use the same number, eliminating the need to manage a separate TIN.
Improved Record Accuracy: Integrating taxpayer records with NIRA data will help reduce duplicate records, errors, and outdated information, resulting in a more accurate and reliable taxpayer register.
Simplified Access to Services: The use of a single identifier will make it easier for taxpayers to access services and comply with tax obligations, including filing returns, conducting land transactions, opening bank accounts, and obtaining tax clearance certificates.
Enhanced Revenue Mobilization: A more accurate and comprehensive taxpayer database will improve visibility of economic activities, strengthen compliance monitoring, and support efforts to reduce tax evasion.
What is changing, and for whom?
Dear Reader,
The transition from the Tax Identification Number (TIN) to the National Identification Number (NIN) introduces the following changes:
a) For Ugandan Citizens
National Identification Number (NIN): The NIN issued by NIRA will become the official tax identifier for individual taxpayers.
Citizens will no longer be required to use a separate 10-digit TIN for tax identification purposes.
b) For Non-Individual Entities
Entity Registration Number (ERN) / Business Registration Number (BRN): Companies, partnerships, associations, and other non-individual entities will use their registration number issued by the Uganda Registration Services Bureau (URSB) as their tax identifier.
This will eliminate the need for a separate TIN for such entities.
c) For Non-Citizens
Alien Identification Number (Alien ID): Non-citizens will use an Alien ID where one has been issued.
In cases where an Alien ID is not available, a tax identification number issued by a foreign tax authority may be used, provided Uganda has a relevant agreement with that jurisdiction.
These changes are intended to create a simpler, more accurate, and efficient taxpayer identification system, while improving service delivery, strengthening compliance, and enhancing the integrity of taxpayer records.
Do I lose my TIN?
Dear Reader,
No, you will not lose your TIN. However, effective 1 st January 2027, taxpayers whose records have been updated will access their TIN accounts using their National Identification Number (NIN) or Entity Registration Number (ERN). The TIN will remain valid; only the login and identification process will change to make taxpayer verification easier, faster, and more secure.
I don’t have a NIN. Can I still register for tax?
Dear Reader,
You are required to obtain a National Identification Number (NIN) from NIRA before registering for a Taxes. If you do not yet have a NIN, please visit the nearest NIRA office for assistance with registration and issuance.
